subtitle: Describing words that become nouns, and little es-chunks
words.intro: On 31 December Germans watch a short black-and-white English sketch that nobody in England knows, set off a small war in the street, and wish each other *alles Gute*.

grammar[0].blocks[0].title: Picture an invisible noun
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: The ending is the one the describing word would have before that noun.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: One word, three people
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: Neuter ones name ideas: *das Gute, das Wichtigste, alles Gute* (all the best). After etwas, nichts, viel: -es — *nichts Besonderes*.
grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: Fireworks may be sold only on the last three working days of the year, and let off only on 31 December and 1 January. Those two days make up a good share of the year’s particulates, and every year a loud argument follows about banning them.

grammar[1].blocks[2].title: es gibt is always gibt
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: Es *gibt* einen Park, es *gibt* viele Cafés — singular, whatever follows. The thing after it takes den, einen.
grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: German lucky charms for the New Year: a pig, a four-leaf clover, a chimney sweep, a horseshoe, a mushroom. You give them to each other at midnight, usually in marzipan. Bakers and sweet shops sell them all week.

listen.intro: A radio survey on free time: people in the street say what they do. Listen for es gibt, es lohnt sich and their opinions.
speak.intro: Tell the tutor your resolutions for next year. What would you change? Which ones are worth it?
canDo[0]: use der Deutsche, die Deutschen correctly
canDo[3]: get through a German New Year’s Eve
opener.caption: Silvester am Brandenburger Tor: Es knallt in der ganzen Stadt.
document.intro: A real cartoon from an old German magazine. It shows *Bleigießen*: at New Year you melt a little lead and drop it in cold water, and the shape tells your future. Read the two lines under the picture.
document.fact: Real lead was banned for this in the EU in 2018, so *Wachsgießen*, with wax, has taken its place. People go on reading the shapes, and each one looks like a boat.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Complete each chunk with gibt, geht, lohnt or kommt.
reading.intro: New Year’s Eve at Lena’s. Max has never seen *Dinner for One*, and the Germans are shocked. Frau Huber has brought her collection of good-luck charms. And Maya has made a list of resolutions, which she intends to read out to everyone.
reading.photos[1].caption: Berliner: Einer davon ist vielleicht mit Senf.
reading.fact: *Dinner for One* was recorded in Hamburg in 1963, in English, and has been shown on German TV on New Year’s Eve ever since. It has been shown thousands of times and most Britons have never heard of it. A typical Sylvester also includes a jam doughnut with a mustard surprise.
